name: Kanchenjunga Falls
tagline: A tall, two-pronged waterfall on the Pelling–Yuksom road
meta_description: Kanchenjunga Falls: a tall roadside waterfall about 28 km from Pelling on the road to Yuksom, flowing all year. Timings, steps, costs and how to combine it.
summary: Kanchenjunga Falls is a tall, double-pronged waterfall beside the Pelling–Yuksom road in Gyalshing district (West Sikkim), about 28 km and 1–1.5 hours from Pelling. It flows all year and is fullest from July to October. A short climb of about 100 steps leads from the car park to the viewing area. Allow 30–45 minutes.
intro: Kanchenjunga Falls drops down a steep, forested cliff above the road between Pelling and Yuksom, in several tiers that split into two main streams. Wikipedia's article on Pelling describes it as the 'imposing double-pronged' falls, about 28 km from Pelling and 18 km beyond the Rimbi river, and notes that it runs throughout the year. The Gyalshing district administration lists it as a primary attraction, open from 8 am to 5 pm.

It is a roadside stop, not a hike. From the parking area a flight of about 100 steps, by the district's count, climbs to a viewing platform close enough to feel the spray in the wet months. There are small cafes and stalls by the road, and the district lists parking and a public toilet, which makes it an easy stop for families. It is one of the busiest single stops in West Sikkim in season.

Almost everyone sees it on the Pelling–Yuksom day tour, together with Rimbi waterfall, Khecheopalri Lake and the Norbugang throne at Yuksom. The falls are fullest during and just after the monsoon, from July to October, and thinner but clearer in the dry months. It is worth ten quiet minutes even on a rushed day. If you are staying in Yuksom, 12 km on, you can return early in the morning, before the tour cars arrive, and have the platform almost to yourself.

story.title: A waterfall named after the guardian mountain
story.text: The falls do not come straight off Kangchenjunga, which stands more than 30 km to the north, beyond the ridges of Khangchendzonga National Park. The water comes from streams on the forested slopes above the road. Why, then, the name? In Sikkim, Kangchenjunga is more than a view. It is worshipped as Dzö-nga, the guardian deity of the land, honoured each year at the festival of Pang Lhabsol, and its Tibetan name is usually translated as 'the five treasures of the high snow', as Wikipedia's article on the mountain explains. Naming a waterfall on the road towards Yuksom, the old capital and gateway to the mountain's park, after Kangchenjunga ties a roadside stop to that wider sacred landscape, which the Buddhist tradition calls Demazong. We have not found a written record of when or by whom the name was first used, so we do not offer one. What you can do is stand on the platform, look up at the water and remember that, for many Sikkimese, the mountain it is named after is watching over the valley.

little_known.fact: The Gyalshing district administration's 2023 survey lists Kanchenjunga Waterfalls as non-ticketed, open 8 am to 5 pm daily, with parking, cafes and a public toilet.
Wikipedia's Pelling article places the falls about 18 km beyond the Rimbi river and about 28 km from Pelling, and says they run throughout the year.
Phamrong Falls, another tall waterfall listed by the district, lies near Tsong village, about 42 km from Gyalshing, on the Yuksom side of the district.

facts: Jul–Oct for flow; Oct–Nov and Mar–May for travel
Tall two-pronged falls, flowing all year
Not needed for Indians; foreigners need the Sikkim RAP

highlights.title: The climb to the viewing area
highlights.text: About 100 steps lead up from the car park to a platform close to the base of the falls. It takes five to ten minutes at an easy pace. In the wet months spray blows across the steps, so wear shoes with grip and hold the railing.

highlights.title: Fullest after the monsoon
highlights.text: From July to October the falls run at full force in two broad white streams, loud enough to drown conversation. September and October are the best balance: strong flow, fewer road problems than mid-monsoon and the first clear skies of autumn.

highlights.title: Part of the Pelling–Yuksom day
highlights.text: The falls sit on the main road to Yuksom, so they slot into a full-day tour with Rimbi waterfall, Khecheopalri Lake and the Norbugang throne and Kathok Lake in Yuksom. Indicatively ₹3,500–5,000 a car from Pelling.

highlights.title: Roadside tea and snacks
highlights.text: Small cafes and stalls by the car park sell tea, coffee, momos, noodles and packaged snacks. Prices are a little above village rates. It is a good mid-morning stop on the way to Yuksom, before the climb to Norbugang.

highlights.title: Quiet early or late
highlights.text: Tour cars arrive in waves from late morning. If you are staying in Yuksom, stop early in the day or in the late afternoon, when the platform is quieter and the light falls more softly on the water.

how_to_reach.text: Shared jeeps between Gyalshing or Pelling and Yuksom pass the falls a few times a day, mostly in the morning, indicatively ₹100–200 a seat. Ask to be dropped, but the next jeep may be hours away, so most budget travellers join a shared day tour from Pelling instead, about ₹500–800 a seat in season.

From Pelling, about 28 km and 1–1.5 hours via Rimbi. A full-day car covering the falls, Khecheopalri Lake and Yuksom costs indicatively ₹3,500–5,000. From Yuksom, about 12 km and 30–40 minutes. From Gangtok, about 140 km and 6–7 hours via Legship and Pelling.

About 165 km and 6.5–7.5 hours via Melli, Jorethang, Legship and Pelling, indicatively ₹6,500–8,500 by private car. Travellers usually see the falls on the way to Yuksom or on a day tour from Pelling. NH10 closes after heavy rain; the alternative is via Darjeeling. Check current status before you travel.

costs: Listed as non-ticketed; parking or small fees may apply
Tea and snacks at the falls
where_to_stay: There is nowhere to stay at the falls. Most travellers stay in Pelling, about 28 km away: Hotel Garuda and Summit Newa Regency are budget and value bases, Norbu Ghang Retreat and Spa suits a comfort trip and The Elgin Mount Pandim is the premium choice. If you are heading to Yuksom, 12 km on, Yuksum Residency and Hotel Tashigang are practical value hotels, and village homestays in Yuksom cost less and include meals.
tips: Wear shoes with grip; the steps are wet and slippery with spray from July to October.
Visit early or late in the day to avoid the late-morning wave of tour cars.
Keep to the platform and do not climb on the rocks at the base; they are wet and very slippery.
Carry a light rain jacket in the wet months to protect yourself and your camera from spray.
Combine the falls with Khecheopalri Lake and Yuksom rather than making a special trip.

experiences.title: Climb the steps to the falls
experiences.best_time: Jul–Oct for flow; daytime 8 am–5 pm
experiences.cost: Free; small parking or entry fee possible
experiences.summary: Stop at the car park on the Pelling–Yuksom road and climb about 100 steps to the viewing area beneath Kanchenjunga Falls, where the water drops in tiers and two main streams, close enough to feel the spray.
body: The Gyalshing district administration lists Kanchenjunga Waterfalls as a primary attraction, open 8 am to 5 pm, with a short climb of about 100 steps from the car park. The climb is easy for most people and takes five to ten minutes, with railings and resting spots.

At the top you stand below a long, tiered drop down a forested cliff. In the monsoon and just after, the water splits into two thundering streams and the spray soaks anyone close to the front. In the dry months, November to May, the flow is gentler and you can see the rock layers behind the water.
Stay on the platform. The rocks at the base are wet, mossy and slippery, and climbing them for photographs is not safe. Carry a rain jacket for spray, and a cloth for your camera lens.

faqs.q: How many steps are there at Kanchenjunga Falls?
faqs.a: The district administration describes a short climb of about 100 steps from the car park to the viewing area. Most people manage it in five to ten minutes. The steps are wet and slippery in the rainy months, so wear shoes with grip and use the railings. Older travellers can rest partway.

faqs.q: Is there an entry fee at Kanchenjunga Falls?
faqs.a: The district's 2023 survey lists the falls as non-ticketed. A parking charge or small fee may be collected at times by the local committee. Check current status before you travel. There are cafes and a public toilet near the car park.

faqs.q: What are the opening hours of Kanchenjunga Falls?
faqs.a: The district administration lists 8 am to 5 pm, every day of the week. In practice the falls are beside a public road, but the stalls, toilet and parking work to these hours. Visit in daylight only; the steps and road are not safe after dark.

experiences.title: Pelling to Yuksom day tour via the falls
experiences.best_time: Oct–Dec and Mar–May; Sep for full falls
experiences.summary: The classic full-day tour from Pelling: Rimbi waterfall, Khecheopalri Lake, Kanchenjunga Falls and Yuksom's Norbugang throne and Kathok Lake, by private car, with time for tea at the falls and a walk at each stop.
body: Leave Pelling by 8 am. The road drops past Darap to Rimbi waterfall and the Rimbi river, then climbs to the turn for Khecheopalri Lake, sacred to Buddhists and Hindus, where a short forest walk leads to the water. Back on the main road, Kanchenjunga Falls is the next stop: climb the steps, have tea, and continue to Yuksom.
In Yuksom, walk up to the Norbugang throne, where the first Chogyal was consecrated in 1642, and around Kathok Lake. If time allows, start back by 2–3 pm to reach Pelling before dark.
Indicatively ₹3,500–5,000 for a private car. In season, shared seats on fixed tours cost about ₹500–800. A night in Yuksom adds Dubdi Monastery and a far easier pace.

faqs.q: What does the Pelling–Yuksom day tour cover?
faqs.a: Usually Rimbi waterfall, Khecheopalri Lake, Kanchenjunga Falls, and in Yuksom the Norbugang coronation throne and Kathok Lake. Some drivers add a tea stop in Darap village. It is about 80 km of hill road in total, so it is a full day; start by 8 am.

faqs.q: How much does a Pelling–Yuksom day tour cost?
faqs.a: Indicatively ₹3,500–5,000 for a private small car for the day from Pelling, and about ₹500–800 per seat on shared tours in season. Entry fees at Khecheopalri Lake and elsewhere are small extras. Prices rise in peak weeks; check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Should I do Yuksom as a day trip or stay overnight?
faqs.a: A day trip covers the main stops but feels rushed and leaves out Dubdi Monastery. A night in Yuksom lets you see the falls and lake on the way, walk to Dubdi the next morning and go on to Tashiding. We recommend at least one night if you have the time.

experiences.title: Two big falls: Kanchenjunga and Phamrong
experiences.summary: From a base in Yuksom, see the district's two best-known big waterfalls in one half day: Kanchenjunga Falls on the Pelling road and Phamrong Falls near Tsong village on the Yuksom side, both at their fullest after the monsoon.
body: The Gyalshing district administration lists two waterfalls among its primary attractions: Kanchenjunga Waterfalls on the Pelling–Yuksom road, and Phamrong Waterfalls, near Tsong village, about 42 km from Gyalshing. If you are staying in Yuksom, both are within reach in half a day by car.

Go from late August to October, when the water is high and the roads have usually reopened after the worst of the monsoon. Start with Kanchenjunga Falls in the morning, before the tour cars from Pelling arrive, then drive to Phamrong, where the setting is quieter and more forested.
Ask your driver about the state of the Phamrong approach before you set out, as conditions change after rain. Check current status before you travel. Wear shoes with grip and carry rain gear.

faqs.q: Where is Phamrong waterfall?
faqs.a: The district administration places Phamrong Waterfalls near Tsong village, about 42 km from Gyalshing, on the Yuksom side of the district. It is reached by reserved taxi, and is quieter than Kanchenjunga Falls. Ask your Yuksom host or driver about the current state of the road before going.

faqs.q: Which is better, Kanchenjunga Falls or Phamrong Falls?
faqs.a: Kanchenjunga Falls is easier to reach, right on the main road with steps, cafes and toilets, and fits any Pelling–Yuksom day. Phamrong is quieter and more forested but needs a separate drive. If you see only one, choose Kanchenjunga Falls; if you are staying in Yuksom, try both.

faqs.q: When are waterfalls in West Sikkim at their best?
faqs.a: From July to October, during and just after the monsoon, when flow is highest. September and October are the best balance of strong water and usable roads. From November to May the falls are thinner but the skies are clearer and travel is easier.

experiences.title: Photographing the falls in full flow
experiences.best_time: Late Aug–Oct, morning or late afternoon
experiences.summary: Photograph Kanchenjunga Falls when it runs fullest, in late August to October, using a tripod and slow shutter for soft water, protecting your gear from spray and timing your visit outside the late-morning crowds of tour cars.
body: The falls photograph best when the water is high and the light is soft. Late August to October gives strong flow with a better chance of usable roads than mid-monsoon. Come early in the morning or in the late afternoon, when tour groups thin out and the light is less harsh on the white water.

A small tripod and a shutter speed of around half a second to a few seconds turn the falls into soft streams; a neutral density filter helps in bright light. Include a railing, a tree or a person on the platform for scale. A wide angle captures both prongs; a short telephoto picks out the tiers.
Spray reaches far in the wet months. Keep a cloth and a rain cover for your camera, and set up where you do not block the steps.

faqs.q: Can I use a tripod at Kanchenjunga Falls?
faqs.a: Generally yes, as long as you do not block the steps or platform for other visitors. In busy hours, late morning in particular, use a small travel tripod or a railing for support. Early morning and late afternoon give the space and light for longer exposures.

faqs.q: What is the best time of day to photograph the falls?
faqs.a: Early morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer and the platform quieter. Midday light is harsh on white water and tour cars crowd the car park. In the monsoon, overcast light is often ideal for even exposures, though rain and spray need care.

faqs.q: Is it safe to visit Kanchenjunga Falls in the monsoon?
faqs.a: The viewing area is safe if you stay on the platform and steps, but the roads from Pelling and to Yuksom can be blocked by slides from June to September. Keep a flexible plan, travel in daylight and ask your driver about conditions. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Where is Kanchenjunga Falls?
faqs.a: Kanchenjunga Falls is beside the main road between Pelling and Yuksom in Gyalshing district (West Sikkim), about 28 km and 1–1.5 hours from Pelling and about 12 km before Yuksom. It is a short climb of about 100 steps from the roadside car park to the viewing area.

faqs.q: Is Kanchenjunga Falls worth visiting?
faqs.a: Yes, as a stop on the Pelling–Yuksom road. It is one of the tallest and most powerful roadside waterfalls in West Sikkim, especially from July to October, and takes only 30–45 minutes. It is not worth a special trip on its own; combine it with Khecheopalri Lake and Yuksom.

faqs.q: How far is Kanchenjunga Falls from Pelling?
faqs.a: About 28 km by road, roughly 1–1.5 hours via Rimbi. A private car day tour covering the falls, Khecheopalri Lake and Yuksom costs indicatively ₹3,500–5,000 from Pelling, and shared tour seats about ₹500–800 in season. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Does Kanchenjunga Falls flow all year?
faqs.a: Yes. Wikipedia's Pelling article describes it as active throughout the year. Flow is strongest from July to October, during and after the monsoon, and lower from December to April, when the falls are thinner but still attractive and the roads are more reliable.

faqs.q: Is the water from Kangchenjunga?
faqs.a: No. Despite the name, the falls are fed by streams on the forested slopes above the road, not by the mountain's glaciers. Kangchenjunga stands more than 30 km to the north. The name honours the mountain, which is worshipped in Sikkim as the guardian deity Dzö-nga.

faqs.q: Are there toilets and food at Kanchenjunga Falls?
faqs.a: The district administration lists parking, cafes and a public toilet. Small stalls sell tea, coffee, momos, noodles and snacks, at prices a little above village rates. Facilities are basic and may close early in the off-season, so carry water and a snack.

faqs.q: Can children and older people visit Kanchenjunga Falls?
faqs.a: Yes. The climb is about 100 steps with railings, manageable for most children and older travellers with rests. Hold children's hands on the wet steps and keep them off the rocks at the base. Those who cannot climb can still see the lower part of the falls from the road.

faqs.q: Can I swim or bathe at Kanchenjunga Falls?
faqs.a: No. The pool and rocks at the base are slippery, the water is cold and fast, and climbing beyond the platform is dangerous, especially in the monsoon. Enjoy the falls from the viewing area. If you want a quiet spot by water, Kathok Lake in Yuksom is a short drive on.

faqs.q: How do I reach Kanchenjunga Falls without a private car?
faqs.a: Join a shared day tour from Pelling in season, about ₹500–800 a seat, or take a shared jeep on the Pelling–Yuksom route and ask to be dropped at the falls. Return jeeps are infrequent and full by afternoon, so a shared tour is easier for most travellers.
